newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to discuss transport of Azeri oil.
newsitem.headline: Russia to discuss transport of Azeri oil.

text.p: Russian officials left for the Azeri capital Baku on Monday for talks on transporting Azeri oil across Russia, the official Itar-Tass news agency said.

The Russian delegation, headed by Deputy Prime Minister Valery Serov, who is in charge of relations with other former Soviet republics, will discuss the timetable for carrying oil and the volumes to be transported, it said.

The delegation includes Minister for Commonwealth of Independent States Affairs Aman Tuleyev, Deputy Energy Minister Anatoly Shatalov and the heads of Russia's biggest oil company NK LUKoil and of its national pipeline company Transneft.
Transneft is currently studying Azeri proposals to pump 70,000 tonnes of Azeri crude in the first quarter of this year, Tass said, quoting Transneft sources.
The state of the pipeline linking Baku and Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk via the Chechen capital Grozny would make it possible to start transporting oil in the near future, they said.
A series of technical questions which have not yet been resolved could be settled in a short period, they said.

The Azerbaijan International Operating Co (AIOC), an $8 billion project grouping 13 international oil companies to develop Azeri fields in the Caspian Sea, plans to start producing "early" oil in August this year.
Tass said the Baku-Grozny-Novorossiisk pipeline could eventually carry about five million tonnes of oil a year (about 100,000 barrels per day) of early oil.
AIOC plans to raise output from its three fields to 700,000-800,000 bpd by 2010.
Tass said Azerbaijan had asked Russia to transport not only the early oil but also the main amounts through the pipeline.

Tass said security guarantees for the sector of the pipeline running through Chechnya had not yet been reached. Russian officials say the terms of a final settlement with breakaway Chechnya will include an agreement on pipeline security.
AIOC also plans to use an alternative route for its early oil via Georgia's Black Sea outlet of Batumi.
